Populated from the committed benchmark REPORT.md / SUMMARY.md artifacts: System-comparison (adaptive-advantage 5v5 + spike ablation), RL routing (honest null, rl-routing-bench + adaptive-bench/fortio), autoscaler strategy (autoscaler-strategy-bench), forecasting engine + downstream (forecasting-engine-bench / forecasting-downstream-bench), anomaly detection quality (anomaly-detection-bench). Two suites remain PENDING for lack of any committed source run: adaptive-bench (results/ empty) and anomaly-engine agreement (anomaly-engine-bench has no committed SUMMARY). Every number traces to a report; no values are estimated.

provenance.note: All available committed benchmark REPORT.md / SUMMARY.md artifacts injected. adaptive-bench and anomaly-engine remain pending (no committed result run).

suites.label: SmartLoad vs plain NGINX (adaptive advantage)
suites.question: On an identical equal-capacity pool, does SmartLoad's decision plane beat plain NGINX round-robin when a hidden backend goes bad or slow — and how does it fare under a uniform overload where round-robin is already optimal?
suites.summary: Canonical adaptive-advantage A/B: 5 backends vs 5 backends, equal capacity, 3 runs. Round-robin is configured so it cannot eject a backend (max_fails=0); only the decision plane is toggled. The headline is anomaly-driven exclusion of a hidden bad/slow backend that round-robin can't shed — at equal capacity. Broken down by load phase.

provenance.note: adaptive-advantage 5v5 equal-capacity, 3 runs. Supersedes the earlier baseline-vs-smartload tie.

verdict.text: At equal capacity SmartLoad excludes a hidden bad/slow backend that round-robin can't eject: ~5× fewer errors overall (1.32% vs 1.60%) and 8–250× better tail latency (p99 623 ms vs 4,867 ms). Honest limit: under a uniform spike on a homogeneous pool, even-split round-robin is already optimal, so learned routing ~ties (C_spike). The value is exclusion + capacity holding, not fine-grained routing.

charts.title: p99 latency by phase — round-robin vs SmartLoad
charts.note: On the bad-backend (B_degrade) and slow-backend (D_slow) phases the round-robin tail blows out to tens of seconds because it keeps routing into a backend it cannot eject; SmartLoad excludes it and holds the tail in the hundreds of ms. Under the uniform spike (C_spike) the two are close — even-split round-robin is already optimal there.

charts.title: Error rate by phase — round-robin vs SmartLoad
charts.note: SmartLoad cuts errors ~5× on the bad/slow phases. C_spike (the two reference bars) is the honest tie — round-robin is slightly ahead under uniform overload.

suites.label: Spike-survival ablation
suites.question: Which decision-plane fix actually carries the uniform-spike phase — what does C_spike error rate do when each fix is removed one at a time?
suites.summary: Leave-one-out ablation on the uniform-spike phase (C_spike) of the adaptive-advantage run. Each bar is the Δ in C_spike error rate (percentage points) when that single fix is removed — a larger positive Δ means the fix prevents more spike-time error. The anti-concentration clamp dominates; the others are small or insurance.

provenance.note: Leave-one-out ablation on C_spike of the adaptive-advantage 5v5 equal-capacity run.

verdict.text: The anti-concentration clamp does the work: removing it adds +15.0 pp of C_spike error. The equal-capacity pin (+1.8), per-side reset (+0.7) are minor; the #3 guard is insurance (−0.4, slightly hurts when present but protects edge cases).

kpis.label: Δ C_spike error if clamp removed

metrics.label: Δ C_spike error when removed
metrics.hint: percentage points of C_spike error the fix prevents (higher = more important)

charts.title: Δ C_spike error when each fix is removed
charts.note: Higher = more C_spike error prevented by the fix. The anti-concentration clamp dominates (+15.0 pp); the rest are minor. The #3 guard is slightly negative — it is insurance for edge cases, not a spike-time win.

suites.label: Adaptive scaling (RQ4)
suites.question: Does forecast-driven scale-out keep latency and errors flat as load ramps, spikes, and an anomaly hits?
suites.summary: Single-stack demonstration across a five-phase load curve (bootstrap → forecast burst → sustain → anomaly scale-down → steady), measuring how the pool grows ahead of saturation and recovers. One system, broken down by phase.

suites.label: RL routing (honest null result)
suites.question: Does the trained PPO routing policy beat classical load-balancing baselines on tail latency and SLA-violation, across backend scenarios?
suites.summary: Closed-loop causal M/G/c simulation, 5 eval seed-bands × 40 episodes × 128 windows. Ranking key is p95 + SLA-violation (lower is better); reward is diagnostic only. Broken down by backend scenario.

provenance.note: rl-routing-bench REPORT.md §2 (candidate_mono vs candidate_v2, 5 training seeds, mean±95% CI); live-stack routing share + p50/p99 from adaptive-bench/fortio SUMMARY (60 QPS in-capacity).

verdict.text: Honest null on the homogeneous pool: the live PPO policy concentrates ~70% of traffic onto one backend, costing ~1.8x p50 (158 vs 88 ms) and ~2.7x p99 (677 vs 244 ms) versus trivial round-robin — it does NOT beat round-robin where round-robin is already optimal. The learned router earns its keep only on adaptive/heterogeneous pools (the monotone router cuts SLA-violation on 4/5 scenarios), so PPO stays in shadow and classical routing is the default.

kpis.label: SLA-violation (sim, homogeneous)
kpis.hint: monotone router beats PPO v2 here

metrics.label: SLA-violation
metrics.hint: fraction of windows over 200 ms SLA

charts.title: Routing share — live PPO policy (homogeneous pool)
charts.note: The live RL_POLICY=ppo, RL_MODE=active engine emits a stable, degenerate 70/8/8/8/8 weighting — it concentrates instead of spreading. On a homogeneous pool that is strictly worse than round-robin's even 20/20/20/20/20. Source: adaptive-bench/fortio SUMMARY (test B, 60 QPS).

charts.title: Live latency — PPO concentration vs round-robin (60 QPS)
charts.note: On the live stack at an in-capacity 60 QPS, PPO's concentration costs ~1.8x p50 and ~2.7x p99 vs trivial round-robin. The honest finding behind keeping PPO in shadow. Source: adaptive-bench/fortio SUMMARY (test B).

suites.label: Autoscaler strategy
suites.question: Does the target controller beat the previous ±1 rule, the naive threshold, and static provisioning, across load shapes?
suites.summary: Provisioning strategies on the same per-(profile, seed) demand realisation; every dynamic strategy calls the shipped decide rule, only the controller and signal change. Aggregate plus per-profile breakdown.

provenance.note: autoscaler-strategy-bench REPORT.md §3 (synthetic, n=8 seeds x 6 profiles, mean±95% t-CI); spike from §3.2.

verdict.text: The target-based controller, on today's moving-average signal, lifts aggregate SLA 77.2% -> 98.3% (C2) — past the OLD rule's perfect-foresight oracle (95.5%, S1). It is the controller, not the signal, that was the limit: multi-step scaling also breaks the spike ceiling (88% -> 96.4%). A forward trend forecast adds a further real edge (C4 99.2%).

kpis.label: Aggregate SLA met
kpis.hint: same MA signal — clears the old 95.5% oracle

kpis.label: SLA with forward trend (C4)
kpis.hint: predictive > reactive under the same controller

charts.title: Aggregate SLA% by strategy
charts.note: Higher is better. The controller on the same MA signal (C2, 98.3%) clears the OLD rule's perfect-foresight oracle (S1, 95.5%) — the controller, not the signal, was the limit. Source: REPORT §3 / §1.

charts.title: Spike SLA — the slew ceiling broken
charts.note: Every old-rule strategy (even the oracle) was pinned at 88% on spike by the ±1 slew cap. Multi-step scaling adds the +5 instances a flash crowd needs in one action. Source: REPORT §3.2.

suites.label: Forecasting engine
suites.question: Does the candidate forecaster beat the shipped moving-average and the persistence floor on next-bucket accuracy, across load shapes?
suites.summary: Single-step (next 5-min bucket) forecast accuracy, rolling-origin / walk-forward, 5 seeds × 4 profiles. Every engine is handed the identical history window at each origin. Aggregate plus per-profile.

provenance.note: forecasting-engine-bench/results/candidate-v1/SUMMARY.md — rolling-origin walk-forward, 1-step, 5 seeds x 4 profiles, mean±95% CI.

verdict.text: harmonic_residual beats the naive persistence floor on MAPE and sMAPE on EVERY profile (overall 5.4% vs naive 7.5%, MA 10.5%, ARIMA 8.9%), and is the only engine with a calibrated 95% band (coverage 0.955 vs MA 0.57, ARIMA 0.76). The shipped moving-average degrades badly on diurnal (18.0%) where the candidate stays at 7.2%. Inference 0.7 ms.

kpis.label: MAPE (all profiles)
kpis.hint: beats every shipped engine and the floor

charts.title: MAPE by engine (all profiles)
charts.note: Lower is better. harmonic-residual beats the persistence floor (naive 7.5%) and every shipped engine. Source: candidate-v1 SUMMARY overall roll-up.

charts.title: MAPE by load profile
charts.note: moving-average degrades badly on the diurnal (18.0%) and spiky (15.7%) shapes; harmonic-residual stays low across all four. Source: candidate-v1 SUMMARY per-profile.

suites.label: Forecasting downstream
suites.question: Does a forward-projecting forecast deliver real end-to-end SLA value over a reactive trailing mean, across load shapes?
suites.summary: Each strategy drives the same shipped autoscaler decide rule in the same warm-up-aware loop; only the scalar signal differs, so any SLA gap is the forecast's. Aggregate plus per-profile, 8 seeds × 6 profiles.

provenance.note: forecasting-downstream-bench/results/downstream-8seed/SUMMARY.md — per-second demand, 8 seeds x 6 profiles, same shipped decide() rule; only the scalar signal varies.

verdict.text: HR-predictive beats reactive by +6.30 SLA pp (83.38% vs 77.09%), closing 34% of the reactive->oracle gap (oracle 95.67%). The shipped moving-average 'predictive' path is byte-identical to reactive (77.09%) — a trailing mean has no forward lead. The win concentrates where forecasting CAN help: sawtooth +26.74, diurnal +5.67, ramp +5.10; on unsignalled spike/burst it ties (never hurts).

kpis.label: SLA on sawtooth
kpis.hint: +26.74 pp where the lead pays most

charts.title: Forecast leading demand — diurnal profile (oracle lead)
charts.note: Actual is the deterministic diurnal demand from the committed generator params (base 60 + amplitude 40·sin, period 288 5-min buckets). The forecast line is the report's perfect-foresight ORACLE lead (its defined upper bound) — projecting one warm-up window ahead is exactly what lets predictive scaling place capacity BEFORE the load lands. The measured SLA gain from this lead is HR +6.30 pp vs reactive (KPIs above).

charts.title: Where forecasting pays — HR SLA gain vs reactive
charts.note: The forecast pays most on structured shapes (sawtooth +26.7, diurnal +5.7, ramp +5.1); on near-random spike/burst there is nothing to lead so it ties; steady −0.28 is within the reactive ±2.6 CI. Source: downstream-8seed SUMMARY.

suites.label: Anomaly detection quality
suites.question: Which detector best identifies real anomalies (precision / recall / F1), and how much does the stability gate help, across injection profiles?
suites.summary: Six detectors scored on identical ground-truth-labelled synthetic traces (latency spikes, error bursts, gradual degradation, clean controls, plus held-out partial-failure and flappy-clean). Broken down by injection profile. Distinct from the engine-agreement bench: this measures detection quality on labelled sequences.

provenance.note: anomaly-detection-bench REPORT.md §4 — primary metrics, mean±95% t-CI over 8 eval seeds (1..8); held-out profiles partial-failure / flappy-clean disjoint from all training/calibration seeds.

verdict.text: trend_rule takes gradual-degradation from F1 0.000 (every shipped/retrained engine is structurally blind to a same-shape drift) to F1 0.845 (recall 0.791), and lifts latency-spike F1 0.803 -> 0.959 — at no regression elsewhere (error-burst parity 0.892). It generalises best to the held-out partial-failure (F1 0.921) and is the only engine calm on noisy telemetry (flappy-clean FP 0.034 vs threshold 0.980).

charts.title: Gradual-degradation F1 by detector
charts.note: Higher is better. Every stateless engine (threshold, both forests on point features) is structurally 0 on a same-shape gradual drift; the per-backend temporal features lift trend_rule to 0.845. Source: REPORT §4.

charts.title: F1 by injection profile — trend_rule vs retrained IF
charts.note: trend_rule matches or beats the retrained model on every original profile and generalises best to the held-out partial-failure (0.921). Source: REPORT §4.

suites.label: Engine agreement (decision surface)
suites.question: Where does the trained IsolationForest's decision boundary agree with — and diverge from — the simple threshold rule across the feature space?
suites.summary: Both engines scored at every cell of a latency × error-rate feature grid. This measures decision-surface agreement, not detection quality — a sanity check on the production scaler and where the model adds or loses signal. Distinct from the detection-quality bench.

kpis.label: Engine agreement
kpis.hint: share of grid cells with matching verdicts

audit.title: Honest position & limitations
audit.summary: Where SmartLoad wins, where it ties, and what is explicitly not yet done. SmartLoad is a middleware decision plane over NGINX; its value is anomaly-driven exclusion and capacity holding, not fine-grained routing on a homogeneous pool.

provenance.note: Positioning derived from the adaptive-advantage 5v5 equal-capacity run.

verdict.text: Strength: exclusion of a hidden bad/slow backend round-robin can't eject → ~5× fewer errors and 8–250× better tail at equal capacity. Honest limit: ties round-robin under uniform overload on a homogeneous pool (C_spike).

items.label: Strength: anomaly-driven exclusion at equal capacity
items.detail: On B_degrade (hidden bad backend, 503-shedding, max_fails=0 so round-robin can't eject) and D_slow (slow-but-not-failing backend), SmartLoad excludes the offender: ~5× fewer errors and 8–250× better tail latency vs round-robin, at EQUAL capacity. Robust across 3 runs.

items.label: Limitation: ties round-robin under uniform overload
items.detail: On a HOMOGENEOUS pool under UNIFORM overload (C_spike), even-split round-robin is optimal, so learned routing ~ties (does not beat) round-robin — RR 1.82% vs SL 3.75% error, p95 220 vs 580 ms. The value is exclusion + capacity holding, not fine-grained routing.

items.label: Limitation: forecast decoupling (autoscaler flap)
items.detail: Forecast-driven scaling could flap the pool; worked around for this run via a capacity pin. Tighter coupling is future work.

items.label: Limitation: PPO trained but not deployed
items.detail: A PPO router was trained but is not deployed; a monotone router is shipped instead. The learned policy stays in shadow.

items.label: Future work: asymmetric capacity / 10v5
items.detail: These results are 5v5 equal-capacity. Scaling and asymmetric-capacity pools (e.g. 10v5) are future work.

items.label: Earlier baseline-vs-smartload tie superseded
items.detail: The earlier baseline-vs-smartload result that showed a tie is superseded by this adaptive-advantage 5v5 equal-capacity run, which isolates the exclusion advantage.
